analysis.title: GS - Pasi - Midterm Election Takeaways - 4 Nov 2026
key_insights: GS Economics says Democrats won majorities in both the House and Senate by much larger margins than expected. Media outlets have called seven Republican-held Senate seats for Democrats (Iowa, Kansas, North Carolina, Ohio, South Carolina, Maine, Texas), enough for a majority.
Alaska is not yet called but prediction markets imply a likely flip, and Mississippi may stay too close to call for several days. If Democrats win both seats they would hold 56 Senate seats.

House popular vote margin is likely D+12-14. Competitive seats such as KY-06 (R+15 for Trump in 2024), FL-14 (R+10), TX-23 (R+15) and FL-22 (R+10) went to Democrats. The swing is consistent with a majority of around 255 seats, though the final count could take days because of California.
The larger majorities could give Democrats slightly more leverage in negotiations with the White House and dilute the influence of small factions within the caucus.

GS expects Democrats to use fiscal deadlines to seek limits on the war with Iran, selected tariff rollbacks, reversal of last year's spending cuts and expanded health benefits. Government funding must be extended and the debt limit raised by next fall.

GS expects Democrats to reverse spending cuts from last year's fiscal package, which would add an estimated 0.25% of GDP to spending in 2027. A deal on discretionary spending or expanded health insurance subsidies would add modestly to that.

The first fiscal test is December 11, when spending authority expires. GS sees a short-term extension to February or March as most likely, but Democrats could seek concessions before taking control. Results generally take effect January 3, 2027, and the Ohio Senate special election result takes effect December 15.
Federal data center and AI regulation outlook is less likely to change, since legislation would still need bipartisan Senate support and would have to overcome a veto.

Democratic wins at the state level are likely to bring short-term data center moratoria. Republicans lost governorships in Texas, Ohio, Nevada, Georgia and Michigan, and Democrats gained a trifecta in Pennsylvania and likely Arizona. GS expects conditional moratoria from Democratic governors in Texas, Georgia and Michigan.

States likely to further restrict data centers account for roughly 45% of planned US data center capacity, with Texas alone at roughly 25%. Follow-on legislation could end certain tax breaks, tighten environmental, water and electricity rules, and make it easier for localities to impose their own moratoria.
GS expects the data center issue to fade in importance because it ranks low among voters' priorities, and expects any moratoria not to be long-lived.

sector_views.rationale: Federal outlook is little changed, but state-level moratoria could affect about 45% of planned US data center capacity expansion in the short term. GS expects them not to last.

risk_factors: State and local data center moratoria could affect about 45% of planned US data center capacity expansion, with Texas around 25%.
Final seat counts remain uncertain: Alaska is uncalled, Mississippi may take days, and California House races could take days to count.
Fiscal deadlines (December 11 funding expiry, debt limit by next fall) give Democrats leverage and raise the chance of brinkmanship.
geopolitical: GS expects Democrats to use fiscal deadlines to seek to limit the war with Iran.
GS expects Democrats to seek rollbacks of selected tariffs.

tension_points.bull_case: GS expects the issue to fade in importance because data centers rank low among voters' priorities, so moratoria would not be long-lived. Federal AI and data center regulation is unlikely to change.
tension_points.bear_case: Democratic governors in Texas, Georgia and Michigan are expected to impose conditional moratoria, and follow-on legislation could end tax breaks and tighten environmental, water and electricity rules. Affected states hold about 45% of planned US capacity.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Moratoria that become long-lived, or new state legislation that ends data center tax breaks and tightens rules, would undercut the view that the issue fades.
